records.name: Netherlands
records.current_summary:
The Netherlands is a very safe destination for transgender visitors. Official guidance prepared for WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 confirms there are no visa or entry restrictions based on gender identity, passports with amended or "X" gender markers are accepted, and no medical documentation is needed. Discrimination based on gender identity is prohibited by law, and a 2025 law makes discriminatory motive an aggravating factor that can increase penalties by a third.

The country's institutions are strongly supportive: Amsterdam operates dedicated LGBTQIA+ reporting networks, and the mayor and police committed to priority investigation of Pride-period incidents in 2026. The capital is among Europe's safer cities for ordinary crime.

One caution: reported discrimination and violence against LGBTQ people has risen sharply since 2022 (anti-trans reports rose about 50% in the last year), and surveys indicate many queer residents avoid public displays of affection. For a visitor this translates mainly to a risk of harassment or verbal abuse, particularly late at night, rather than systematic danger.
records.current_localsOnly: The LGR process (still requires an expert letter, falling short of self-determination; the Transgender Act was withdrawn in July 2025 though debate restarted in December) and the non-binary X court procedure are resident-facing.
records.current_outOfScope: Pickpocketing, bike theft, and taxi scams in Amsterdam affect all tourists.

sources.claim: WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 official safety/travel page: visa requirements depend only on nationality, not gender identity — trans and non-binary visitors are not treated differently in visa applications; passports with a marker different from the birth-assigned sex or an 'X' marker are valid if officially issued, and no extra gender documents are required at the border. The Netherlands ranks #13 on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026. For this record: current official entry/border guidance for trans visitors.

Outright International Netherlands overview (updated March 2026): legal gender change still requires a medical expert letter, falling short of self-determination; the 'X' marker is available only through a court procedure taking 3-9 months; the Transgender Act (self-ID) was withdrawn in July 2025; compensation was offered to people sterilised under earlier rules. For this record: dated status of document-changing rules a trans visitor may care about.

Dutch government page on combating anti-LGBTIQ+ discrimination and violence: over 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence — 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people — and incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence rose sharply per the 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism (in 2022, one third of police discrimination reports concerned sexual orientation). For this record: official victimisation figures for trans people.

Government.nl (laws in force 1 July 2025): a private-member's bill (Timmermans/Bikker) puts discriminatory motive into law as a ground for increasing penalties in criminal cases, alongside expanded victims' rights and protection of victim data. For this record: the aggravating-factor hate-crime mechanism visitors benefit from, in force since 1 July 2025.

Equaldex data for the Netherlands: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change legal but requires medical diagnosis, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover sexual orientation only, discrimination illegal, employment/housing discrimination prohibited on SOGI, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. High public support (52% support LGBT openness; ranked #2 of 121 regions as a 'good place').

NL Times (Apr 2026), police figures via Transgender Netwerk: 4,800 discrimination/violence reports about LGBTQIA+ people last year — up 7.5% on 2024 and up 81% from 2,654 in 2022 — with reports about transgender people up 51% in a year (264 to 399); COC calls it 'extremely worrying', noting only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination last year. For this record: quantified rise in reported anti-LGBTQ incidents with the trans-specific subset.

NL Times (Jul 2026): more than 70 people reported discrimination during the start of WorldPride Amsterdam via the RITA platform — mostly festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and Pride Walk participants — with RITA warning the reports are 'only a fraction of the total'. For this record: documented incident volume during the 2026 Pride itself.

NL Times (Jun 2026): Amsterdam broadened 'Safer Spaces' reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence during World Pride — Nieuwe Kerk, Stedelijk Museum, Stadsarchief, hotels plus a central RITA location — with 1.4 million visitors expected. For this record: the incident-reporting infrastructure a visitor can actually use.

NL Times (Jun 2026): Mayor Halsema told the council Amsterdam will tackle discrimination and violent incidents with priority during World Pride (police/enforcer/organiser agreements to act fast); recent Prides drew 25-45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports (vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation, serious assault), typically with perpetrators fleeing the scene. For this record: baseline Pride-period incident counts and official response posture.

OSCE/ODIHR hate-crime frameworks page for the Netherlands: Dutch legislation contains no statutory definition of 'hate crime', while police record hate crimes, hate speech and other discrimination incidents (data collection by the police Centre of Expertise Discrimination, ECAD-P). For this record: the recording framework behind Netherlands hate-crime statistics.

records.name: United States
records.current_summary:
The United States demands real caution from trans visitors — and uniquely among Western nations, is the subject of official trans-traveler warnings from at least eight European allied governments (Germany, Finland, Denmark, and others, March 2025) following executive orders requiring federal documents to reflect sex assigned at birth. A German traveler, Jessica Brösche, was detained at the US border for weeks and deported (January 2025); a CBP officer faces a lawsuit for alleged sexual contact with a trans traveler at Boston Logan Airport. Trans Americans have been stranded with mismatched passports.

Enforcement extends into daily life: in April 2025 a trans woman was arrested and jailed overnight under Florida's bathroom law — believed to be the first such arrest — and a trans man was detained by police in South Carolina for using a women's restroom. State-level bathroom laws, misgendering statutes, and a hostile federal posture coexist with strong protections in blue states and cities.
records.current_outOfScope: Gun violence, mass-shooter risk, petty theft, and traffic safety are general US travel risks affecting everyone.

sources.claim: A4TE airport-security guide: TSA screening procedures can be invasive of privacy and risk 'outing' trans travelers (secondary screening, devices, pat-downs); practical advice on prohibited items and carry-on limits for trans passengers navigating US checkpoints.

HRW (3 Mar 2026): a US state (Kansas) enacted a law invalidating birth certificates and driver's licenses not matching sex assigned at birth and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; more targeting bills pending in state legislatures; the US Supreme Court recently allowed the State Department to change trans passport treatment.

AP (Feb 2026): 'New law puts Kansas at vanguard of denying trans identities on drivers licenses, birth certificates' — Kansas prevents transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and licenses; rights groups call it a template for other states.

MAP equality map: state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in 9 states + 1 territory; outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states (29 states + 4 territories + D.C. have no such ban); some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances.

USA TODAY (7 Mar 2025): Trump executive order requires all US identity documents to reflect sex assigned at birth; ACLU sued the State Department for seven plaintiffs; trans/nonbinary travelers report passports confiscated or blocked, leaving some stranded abroad.

AP (Apr 2025): 'Transgender student's arrest for violating Florida bathroom law is thought to be a first' — a trans student declared 'I am here to break the law' and was handcuffed in a women's restroom at the state capitol; civil-rights attorneys say it is the first known arrest under the state's bathroom-restriction law.

Lambda Legal FAQ: passport and identity-document rules for TGNCNBI people under federal policy change -- what documentation to consider, how name/gender changes interact with federal records, and current status of document updates.

Erin In The Morning (13 Jul 2026) national risk map: Idaho becomes the latest 'Do Not Travel' state for trans people, now 4 states flagged do-not-travel; 2026 legislative season continued degrading trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends -- dated state-level travel-risk guidance.

HRC (updated 2025): since Jan 2025 executive order, new/renewed US passports show sex assigned at birth regardless of gender identity or name change; the 'X' marker (available since 2022) eliminated; policy challenged in federal courts -- current passport posture for trans US travelers.

CNN (Apr 2025): 'Countries issue advisories about trans people traveling to the United States' — multiple foreign governments warn their trans citizens about travelling to the US over identity-document and data rules.

Axios (March 2025): Trump's transgender rights rollbacks prompt allies to adjust travel warnings - at least eight European countries (including Finland and Denmark) adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the US; advisories follow detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

Vox (17 Mar 2026): the US trans-rights fight entering a new phase beyond sports and youth gender medicine -- policy and legal battles expanding into bathroom restrictions, health-care limits and document rules across states (Kansas among battlegrounds).

MAP identity-document policy map: state driver's licence, birth-certificate and name-change rules for trans people -- which states allow gender marker changes by licence or birth certificate, under what conditions (policy tables, undated).

Queer Compass (27 Apr 2026): US LGBTQ+ travel guide -- no national sodomy law, safety varies by state; covers document risks at entry, state-by-state protections, trans travel concerns and checking recent violence reports before travel.

Condé Nast Traveler (Feb 2025): what to know about the new policy on passport gender markers - the State Department stopped processing X-marker passports and markers not matching sex assigned at birth; existing X-marker passports remain valid until expiration; new applications processed only as M or F per supporting documents.

records.name: Russia
records.current_summary:
Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression — including, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and the US State Department explicitly warns LGBT travellers of this.

The UK Home Office assesses that trans people specifically are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution in Russia. Enforcement has produced over a hundred "extremism" convictions for displaying LGBT symbols or participation, bar raids, and the death in custody of a man who ran travel tours for gay customers. Enforcement focuses on public expression and activism rather than private existence, and same-sex activity itself is not criminalised — a discreet visitor is not automatically targeted — but there is effectively no police protection, and detention carries placement by passport sex.

Chechnya and the wider North Caucasus, where quasi-Sharia governance applies, are in a separate and graver category of danger for anyone perceived as LGBT.
records.current_localsOnly: The 2023 LGR and gender-affirming-care bans are resident-facing; the extremism-designation machinery (convictions, NGO liquidation) targets resident organisations and individuals.
records.current_outOfScope: The US State Department and most Western governments advise against all travel to Russia regardless of any personal characteristic, due to the risk of wrongful detention, the war in Ukraine, and arbitrary law enforcement.

sources.claim: UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation/gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025; page updated 12 Aug 2026): affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia — including the autonomous republic of Chechnya — constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. External-protection framework, dated 2025-26.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying US State Department travel advisory for Russia (Level 4 'Do Not Travel') includes warnings relevant to LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch (30 Jun 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for alleged participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its alleged symbols; the charges span administrative and criminal codes, and HRW calls on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Meduza (19 Jun 2025): after the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the non-existent 'international LGBT movement' as extremist, cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought over 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the past two years alone.

The Moscow Times (23 Jun 2025): arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025 — a St Petersburg queer woman describes waking up to find herself 'a second-class citizen' after the Supreme Court's extremist designation.

AP (Dec 2024): 'Russian man arrested for allegedly running LGBTQ+ travel agency found dead in custody' — detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business, found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

AP (Dec 2024): 'Russia's LGBTQ+ community is living in fear following new laws and court rulings, activists say' — the post-designation crackdown under Putin pushes people into silence, flight and self-censorship.
Foreign Policy (Aug 2024): 'Russia's New Queer Purge: The Court Decision Driving the LGBT Community Into Exile' — how the extremism designation fuelled a purge and mass emigration of LGBT Russians.

BBC Russian (27 Jul 2024): follows 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a Siberian conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk — held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and do manual labour before escaping when police responded to a phone she found — a documented account of coercive conversion practice against trans people in Russia.

Novaya Gazeta Europe (29 Jun 2024): after Putin signed the law prohibiting gender reassignment surgery and legal gender changes on official documents, for many transgender Russians emigration has become the only means of survival; profiles those caught in limbo between leaving and staying.

The Guardian (17 Jan 2024): within 48 hours of the Supreme Court's extremist designation, masked police raided LGBTQ-friendly Moscow bars — about 100 patrons at one venue ordered to face walls, searched and photographed — with at least two other venues raided the same night, showing the speed of the post-ruling crackdown.

records.name: Afghanistan
records.current_summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. The 2024 Morality Law (PVPV) obliges the regime's virtue police to prevent "homosexuality" and "lesbianism"; the Taliban applies the death penalty for same-sex relations under its interpretation of Sharia; and documented practice against LGBTIQ people includes beatings, sexual violence in detention, forced confessions, and house-to-house searches. Transgender Afghans report living in hiding, in windowless rooms, for years.

There is no legal recognition, no protection, no functioning consular protection, and no tourism infrastructure that would allow a visitor to blend in. A discovered trans visitor would face the same enforcement apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: detention with routine sexual and physical abuse of queer detainees, prosecution for moral crimes, and corporal punishment that UN experts say is escalating into 2026.

This is the reference point for the very bottom of the risk scale.
records.current_outOfScope: Armed conflict, terrorism, kidnapping, and the arbitrary detention of foreign nationals for leverage are severe risks for every visitor to Afghanistan, independent of any personal characteristic.

sources.claim: EUAA Country Guidance: Afghanistan, section 3.17 'LGBTIQ persons' (profile last updated Jan 2023, in guidance May 2024): treats LGBTIQ Afghans as persons perceived to transgress religious/social norms, alongside minors without support networks and persons facing the death penalty — the asylum-framework basis for assessing Afghan LGBTIQ protection claims in the EU.

EUAA COI Report — Afghanistan Country Focus, section 4.5 (Feb 2026): no legal protections for sexual orientation or gender identity before or after the 2021 takeover; the 'Morality Law' of 31 Jul 2024 specifically prohibits lesbianism, anal intercourse and enabling same-sex relationships; per Amnesty International, same-sex relations are punishable by death.

Human Rights Watch / OutRight report (Jan 26, 2022), 43 pages based on 60 interviews with LGBT Afghans: Taliban members and their supporters attack, threaten and expel LGBT people from their homes; family, neighbour and partner abuse surged after the takeover; many went into hiding or fled.

OutRight International report (Feb 14, 2023), 22 interviews Sep-Oct 2022 with LGBTIQ Afghans still in-country: Taliban security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in early rule, with physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations — punishments the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed on social media.

DW feature (Oct 2, 2021): profiles a trans man and a gay friend in their mid-20s hiding in Kabul after the Taliban takeover, stating that under Taliban rule LGBTQ people face the death penalty and their only option is to leave; documents street attacks on men coded as gay (clothing changed, confinement indoors).

JURIST feature (Nov 8, 2024) summarising the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan (formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees in Bremen): reports systematic persecution after Aug 2021, noting that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework and that visibly transgender individuals face the gravest risks including exploitation and violence.

Translation of Article 22 of the Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice (PVPV) Law, dated 31 Jul 2024: the overseer must prevent listed 'evils' including lesbianism and homosexuality 'even if with one's own spouse', codifying moral surveillance over same-sex conduct alongside adultery, gambling and other offences.

OHCHR press release (Mar 2026): UN human-rights experts condemn the Taliban's surging use of public corporal punishment — at least 1,110 people flogged in 2025 alone, nearly double 2024 — warning women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for 'moral crimes' such as adultery, 'illicit relationships' and 'sodomy'.

Human Dignity Trust country profile (updated Jan 19, 2026): Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; Penal Code 2017 provisions on 'sodomy' and 'inciting sodomy' carry up to two years, while the Penal Code's Sharia-reference clause allows the death penalty for same-sex activity.
CNN (Nov 2024): 'LGBTQ Afghans say they face abuse in detention as Taliban crackdown intensifies' — first-person accounts of arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody.

records.name: United Kingdom
records.current_summary:
The United Kingdom has a documented, in-force rollback concentrated on facilities and detention that directly affects trans visitors. Bathroom and changing-room use is now directed by biological sex under the Equality watchdog's statutory code — a daily, nationwide civil restriction (the UK is the only country above 0.55 in this dataset with a nationally-legislated bathroom restriction). Since the April 2025 Supreme Court ruling, two severe-when-triggered risks apply if arrested: police forces strip-search trans women according to biological sex (with male officers), and trans women are placed in men's prisons — with documented suicide-risk litigation.

Documented trans killings have occurred (Brianna Ghey, 2023, and others). The climate is actively deteriorating via courts/EHRC-led rollback (not executive demonization — a contrast with the United States).

The UK's traveler-relevant positives are limited: no trans-specific border friction (foreign passports with X or amended markers are accepted), hate-crime law covering gender identity (theoretical recourse), no criminalisation, and functional institutions. The Gender Recognition Certificate and marriage equality — previously cited as positives — are resident-facing and do not apply to visitors.
records.current_localsOnly: The Gender Recognition Certificate regime and marriage equality are resident-facing; the strip-search and men's-prison placement policies apply to resident detainees (and to any visitor arrested).
records.current_outOfScope: Ordinary city crime in London and night-out alcohol incidents affect all travellers.

sources.claim: BBC Scotland (19 Jun 2026): Judge Lady Ross ruled the Scottish Prison Service's guidance — allowing some trans prisoners to be held in jails matching their gender identity rather than sex at birth — unlawful; sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis.

BBC (5 Feb 2026): Court of Session told that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk; For Women Scotland is challenging the Scottish prison guidance (only biological females in the women's estate), government lawyers defending individual risk assessments as flexible.

The Guardian (17 Apr 2025): British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court gender ruling — trans women to be strip-searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; prior policy had let trans women staff intimately search women holding a GRC; Sex Matters welcomed the change.

Police Scotland (25 Jun 2025): interim guidance on searching transgender persons — searches involving removal of more than a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear are conducted on the basis of biological sex (custody and stop-and-search); where lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of the individual's lived gender on request.

UK Constitutional Law Association analysis (16 Jul 2026) of For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59 (Outer House, Court of Session, 19 Jun 2026): critique of the judgment striking down the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory trans-custody guidance, examining Equality Act 2010 Sch.22(1), the Prison Rules, GRA 2004 and the court's Article 8 approach.

BBC (Aug 2026): new EHRC guidance on single-sex spaces has come into force — the code gives organisations practical examples for compliance (Sex Matters' Maya Forstater: 'the law is clear and the code is practical'); Northern Ireland, on different equality legislation, is still assessing the Supreme Court ruling's impact.

TransActual UK 'Gendered Spaces Report 2025': survey of trans, intersex and gender-nonconforming respondents corroborating their fears of harassment from those opposed to their inclusion in public gendered spaces; full report published as PDF.
JURIST (18 Aug 2026): UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying document is Surrey Police's searching/biological-sex policy (FOI release).

records.name: Germany
records.current_summary:
Germany is very safe for transgender visitors, with two real caveats worth knowing. First, far-right street hostility is the most documented concern: roughly 110 of 245 Christopher Street Day (Pride) events in 2025 were disrupted or attacked, over half linked to organised far-right networks — a visitor at Pride, or visibly trans in the eastern Länder, faces elevated harassment. Second, if you are arrested, prison placement follows your self-chosen civil-registry gender entry under recent state-level reforms (better than France, which still places by legal gender/ID and has subjected trans women to gynaecological "verification"), but exceptions allow placement contrary to your self-declared gender and are invoked inconsistently — a neo-Nazi provocateur who self-ID'd to female was reassigned from a women's to a men's prison in 2026 after public outcry.

Offsetting this: bathrooms are unrestricted (venue-level sauna debates only), no border-police humiliation of trans travellers is documented, and carrying personal HRT through the Schengen area is uneventful. The Self-Determination Act (self-ID) is a positive climate signal though not itself a traveller-outing factor.

Calibration note (Aug 2026): Germany recorded a ~35% rise in "gender diversity" hate-crime assaults in 2024 (1,152 cases) and a trans DJ filed an Equal Treatment Act complaint over degrading security screening at Frankfurt Airport — a real airport-outing incident, though resolved through a functioning legal complaint mechanism. Germany simultaneously issued trans-traveler warnings about the US and its Constitutional Court blocked an extradition to Hungary on trans-rights grounds, confirming strong institutional protections.
records.current_localsOnly: The Self-Determination Act's civil-registry procedure and the state-level prison-placement reforms are resident-facing administrative law; the prison-placement exceptions and their inconsistent invocation affect resident detainees.
records.current_outOfScope: General urban crime is low; standard travel precautions suffice. The far-right street activity flagged affects Pride events and some eastern regions disproportionately.

sources.claim: NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying France24 piece (July 2026) covers the German neo-Nazi (legally female under the Self-Determination Act) being sent to a men's prison.

Verfassungsblog essay (March 2026, German) 'Selbstbestimmung hinter Gittern': several German states amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity; new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all; argues trans prisoners need no discriminatory special law — ordinary anti-discrimination law should govern their placement and treatment.

DW feature (23 Aug 2023): German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates — case of climate activist Penelope Frank (Last Generation), legally recorded male who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted; housing runs on a binary men/women model with gender-identity-conforming placement only exceptional.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering Jan–Dec 2025): June — Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia 'safe countries of origin' despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there; July — Education Minister banned gender-inclusive language in her ministry, which the Federal Anti-Discrimination Office said contradicts constitutional equality protection; August — the Merz coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

BBC (20 Aug 2025): where trans far-right extremist Marla-Svenja Liebich (gender entry changed to female end-2024 under the new Self-Determination Act) would serve 18 months for incitement — Halle's chief prosecutor said Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake; press council unanimously rejected her complaint against Der Spiegel as unfounded; a Berlin court rejected her injunction against journalist Julian Reichelt.

DW (16 Jul 2026): after extradition from Czechia, Marla-Svenja Liebich was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025 — authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility; critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law.

Resident Advisor (20 Jun 2025): trans DJ/producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a 23 Nov 2024 Frankfurt Airport screening in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity ('targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment'); she provided RA a copy of her statement to the airport.

German STOP the HATE campaign site (Prevention & Empowerment, northern Germany): counselling-finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting ('Dunkelziffer'), evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels — a practical resource directory for someone facing hostility.

RTL (German, Jan 2025): the Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline restricting women's saunas to persons whose 'primary sex characteristics correspond' set off a debate about registered trans women's access; trans woman Alessia Dorigo countered that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic — identity is felt, not declared, and took a hard road.

Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel (German): how Berlin saunas and similar venues now treat trans women after the Self-Determination Act took effect 1 January 2025 — months of public argument over women-protected spaces with fears the self-declaration route would be misused, intensified by a Deutscher Sauna-Bund statement (paywalled body, lede captured).

Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony (KFN) project page: the German penal system runs on statutory separation (§ 170(2) Lower Saxony correctional act) with binary men/women housing; placement corresponding to gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; the project researches transgender people's situation in prison.
Berlin prison service official page (in German): information for trans, inter and non-binary persons in custody - rules and contacts across Berlin facilities.

freshness_all.fact: Germany's rights level (ranked among Europe's highest) unchanged; sole cited source is the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (Feb 2026), by definition current.

records.name: Japan
records.current_summary:
Japan is a very safe destination for transgender visitors in practice, with a legal framework that lags behind. There is no national anti-discrimination law — the 2023 "understanding" law is symbolic — and legal gender change still requires a court process. But courts have moved in trans people's favour: the Supreme Court struck down the sterilisation requirement for legal gender change in 2023 and ruled workplace bathroom restrictions on a transgender woman illegal the same year.

Day-to-day risk is minimal: violent crime is rare, visibly trans visitors report curiosity more often than hostility, hotels and transport are unproblematic, and Tokyo and Osaka have an established queer scene. The main practical challenge is the strictly gendered, full-nudity culture of hot springs (onsen) — manageable using guides to gender-neutral or private rental baths and mixed open-air baths, which travellers actively share.

One caveat: online transphobic rhetoric and misinformation rose visibly during the 2023 legislative debates, indicating a live culture-war current, though it rarely translates into street-level trouble for visitors.
records.current_localsOnly: The court-based legal gender change process, the 2023 sterilisation ruling, and the workplace-bathroom ruling are resident-facing; the onsen challenge is traveler-facing and stays in the summary.
records.current_outOfScope: Natural disasters (earthquakes, typhoons) are Japan's principal travel risk and affect everyone.

sources.claim: Official translation of Japan's SOGI-promotion Act (Act on Promotion of Public Understanding of Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity): defines 'gender identity', requires the government to publish annual implementation status of policies promoting understanding of SOGI diversity, and sets out the national basic plan — the statutory framework now governing official态度 to LGBT issues.

AP (Jul 2023): 'Japan's top court says government restrictions on transgender employee's use of restrooms illegal' — the Supreme Court upholds damages over a ministry's limits on a trans female employee's toilet access.

AP: 'A Japanese court rules it's unconstitutional to require surgery for a change of gender on documents' — landmark ruling in 'Gen Suzuki's' case against the sterilising-surgery requirement for legal gender-marker changes.

HRW (18 Jul 2023): Japan's Supreme Court ruled the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry violated public-service law by barring a transgender woman from the women's bathroom at work — she challenged the denial in 2015; a Tokyo district court had ruled for her in 2019 on her 'important legal interest' to live by her self-identified gender and awarded damages.

Kyodo News FOCUS (21 Jun 2023): Japan enacted its LGBT-understanding-promotion law after months of debate but the text was watered down amid a culture-war debate over transgender issues — documents the political contestation behind the statute.

Japan Cheapo inclusive-onsen guide: bathhouses (onsen, sento, super-sento) can be daunting for non-binary and trans visitors; provides LGBTQ+-friendly venue recommendations, private-bath and co-ed-pool options, and practical etiquette — a direct visitor-utility page for gender-diverse travelers.

Freely AU first-person guide 'Using onsen in Japan as a trans person' (published 29 Mar 2023, last updated 10 Jul 2026): what to expect using bathhouses as a trans traveller — practical expectations, venue norms and transition-related concerns from lived experience.

Japan Gay Guide visitor outlook: most travelers experience little direct hostility or discrimination, especially in major tourist destinations; LGBTQ visibility is low, social attitudes can be reserved, and legal equality still lags other developed countries — the standard visitor-risk posture for Japan.

Chambers Global Practice Guide update (Japan LGBTQ status): significant progress including enactment of the SOGI-promotion law, two pro-transgender Supreme Court decisions and one gay-friendly Supreme Court decision, while full marriage equality and violence-protection guarantees remain absent — legal-status update useful for framing institutional protection.

CEDAW NGO shadow report on LBT persons in Japan (May 2009): situation characterised by invisibility, marginalisation, silent prejudice and stigmatisation; lesbians, bisexual women and transgender persons face discrimination across education, employment, housing and health care with little governmental attention — dated baseline for institutional-protection claims.

records.name: Ireland
records.current_summary:
Ireland is a calm, comfortable destination for transgender visitors. It was one of the first countries in the world to introduce legal gender recognition by self-declaration — the Gender Recognition Act 2015 lets adults change their legal gender without medical requirements — and bathroom use is unrestricted. A hate-crime law covering sexual orientation and gender identity finally took effect at the end of 2024, equality law bans discrimination in employment, housing and services, and marriage equality was approved by referendum in 2015.

The caveats are stagnation and a mildly worsening climate rather than active rollback. The 2015 law is binary-only and long-promised reform (non-binary, under-16s) has stalled; transphobic hate speech remains uncriminalised after a 2024 government U-turn; a 2025 university study documented rising discrimination against sexual and gender minorities; and total hate-crime reports rose about 15% in 2025 (racism and xenophobia are the most common motives). None of this amounts to criminal exposure or physical danger for a visitor.

Day-to-day, Ireland is welcoming with low violent crime and a strong civil-society support network.
records.current_localsOnly: The Gender Recognition Act 2015 (binary-only, stalled non-binary/under-16 reform) is a resident-facing process.
records.current_outOfScope: No trans-specific travel advisory exists; general urban crime is low.

sources.claim: Guardian (23 Dec 2025): decade retrospective on Ireland's gender recognition — the 2015 Act marked a move away from Ireland's Catholic past; first-person accounts of self-declaration and updated documents, alongside renewed calls over remaining gaps in trans rights and healthcare.

Irish Statute Book: Gender Recognition Act 2015 (No. 25 of 2015) — commenced 4 September 2015 (S.I. 369/2015); the operative statutory text enabling legal gender recognition, later amended per S.I. updates through 2026.

Belong To LGBTQ+ Youth Ireland: hate-crime guidance — anonymous online hate-crime reporting form, rights information and links to Equal Status Acts protections for young LGBTQ+ people reporting incidents.
